Content:
The cats' meat rabbit hole was fascinating! To this day, in Brazil, we call meat skewers of questionable quality "cat skewers" (at least in my region).
If the cats' meat practice was more widespread in Europe (which I presume it was), this might be the origin of the expression!

Author: @mysticlabyss6910
Content: I have been making this exact dish for 50 years. Taught by my German by heritage, Grandmother, who hailed from  Hungary .... go figure. Chicken, I usually go with 2 bone in chicken breast and 2 drumsticks,I I wrap in cheesecloth to keep the icky bits from falling into the sauce but that's optional,  bacon fat, 2  onion, 1 tsp salt, 1 stalk celery (optional) sliced carrot, lots of garlic (6),  sour cream, 2 cartons chicken stock boil down to a thick sauce, takes a couple hours. Maybe a tsp or two of better than chicken boullion or knorr (not bovril) chicken concentrate. Remove chicken before it starts falling off the bone but do wait til it's good and tender. Add sour cream 1/2 cup right before adding dumplings. Add dumplings just before serving.  I make my dumplings with flour, egg water and salt .... 1 egg to 1 cup flour 1/2 tsp salt and enough water to make a gooey but stiff shaggy dough. Easily scalable, 1 cup flour usually makes enough for 2 people. drop by small spoonfuls into boiling water. When they float they are done.  I call it Chicken Paprikash

Author: @jamesverhoff1899
Content:
If you're going to do Vlad, you should also do Elizabeth Bathory. What Vlad was alleged to have done, Elizabeth Bathory did. It's not clear if Stoker was aware of her existence or not--he doesn't mention her in his notes as far as I can tell--but still, she's certainly part of vampire lore. 

I spent some time in Romania, and found their views on Vlad to be interesting. He was something of a folk hero. He was cruel and did very vicious things, sure, but they weren't unwarranted; they were in the service of saving the country from being taken over by people who'd betrayed his family while he was gone fighting wars elsewhere. And for all his cruelty, he didn't reach what his enemies were accused of (which, take with a grain of salt; Medieval stories tend to be expanded upon for effect). The transformation into the vampire Count Dracula was treated a bit like we treat the Salem witches--if you're going to make the area a tourist hot spot, who are they to turn down free money? 

I always miss the Carpathians when I read or watch "Dracula". Of all the mountain ranges I've seen, those are the closest to a fairy tale forest. Absolutely beautiful. And the food....The stuffed cabbages probably took a few years off my lifespan, but the flavor was amazing!

Content: i am Romanian (my country is where Transylvania is located) and this dish is really tasty indeed. I am from the southern part of the country while Transylvania is in the center of it, and we cook the dumplings in a bigger size (like the shape of a spoon), not this small, and we add them to the sauce while its still cooking on the stove along with the meat. Also, SHLIBOVITZA (how we pronounce it) is not a brandy and at times can be made quite strong. Normally its around 40 degrees alcohol but it can reach much more than 60 degrees and then it is usually called PALINCA. And yes, Dracula as we know it (Vlad Dracul The Impaler) has nothing to do with vampires for us. Like most romanians, we heard about the western Dracula vampire version from other countries because for us, Vlad Dracul (meaning the Evil) was a cruel ruler that was merciless to his enemies in the 1400s, impaling them. His castle still exists and it is full of torture tools and machines.

Dracula in Romanian means Little Dragon. Dracul means Dragon and adding the a at the end modifies the word to mean a little or young version. When applied to a person's name it can also mean son/daughter of that person.

As such, Vlad (III) Dracula was the son of a Vlad (II) Dracul. Father was dragon, son was the little dragon. In fact all his sons bore the Dracula surname in a way similar to how more western European groups established surnames like Johnson, ie Son of John.

Author: @jp326williams
Content:
Very good video.  But,  as a Transylvanian resident,  your pronunciation of mamaliga needs a tweek.  It's pronounced Mumma Leegah.  And is served with Sarmale (sarmarlay) at most religious or holiday meals here to this day! 

The Mediaș gold you mention is most likely the Festeasca Neagra grape, or Rara Neagra. 

The plum brandy is called Țuica or Palinca (Tsweeka or Palinka) in Romania. And is made in most villages and served at any opportunity! 

And for anyone wanting to visit and see the actual places Vlad iii is from,  please dont fall for the advertised 'Dracula's Castle' being at Bran,  near Brașov, he almost certainly never set foot in the place (although it's a very pretty castle and former residence of Queen Maria). His real castle was Poenari (about an hour from Bran), his seat of power was Târgoviște and his birthplace was Sighișoara.  All of which are very much worth visiting for their beauty and history...and food! 

Maybe you should try Papanași (Papanash) a delicious 'doughnut' type of ball made from sweet cheese,  lightly fried and served with Smantana (creme freche) and usually a blueberry compote!

Content: We can kind of see how Bram Stoker didn't know much about Transylvania or the historical Dracula when he wrote the book. Early drafts had the vampire come from Styria Austria, the setting of an earlier vampire novel. When he heard a bit ovpf Vlad Draculea he borrowed the name. Of course Vlad Draculea was from Vallachia not Transylvania. In 1897 Transylvania was part of the Hungarian kingdom half of the Empire of Austria-Hungary (aka "Transleithania"). The population was mostly ethically Romanian (as was the historical Dracula) with Hungarian minorites (Stoker makes Dracula a Szelzkey, a Hungarian). The use of German has less to do with Austria (as I said Transylvania was part of Transleithiania the Hungarian kingdom, not Cisleithania the Austrian side) but with the Saxon villages that existed in Transylvania until WWII.

Author: @princessmaly
Content:
A bit aboot the degree to which Stoker consciously based the character on Dracula:

The story goes that Bram Stoker got very in depth into his research for the book and became something of a student on Romanian history because of all the reading, therefore, it should not be taken as a coincidence that he uses the name Vlad signed letters with as the name of the count. There is also a reference to the Impaler in the text, and so, y'know, all this was taken for granted.

What changed is that later on people with better access to primary documents of Stoker's notes and outlines called this into question, because in practice Stoker really only read, like, a couple of books. And remember also that prior to the 70's, when scholarship of Stoker first proposed this connection, most English speaking people in the UK and US hadn't heard of Dracula the person, because his international notoriety kind of stopped at the kind of stories written aboot him in foreign markets which played up his nature as a cruel monster, and to this day we really just don't know how much of that is even true. So in Stoker's time, he did do his due diligence as far as research goes insofar as the novel's subject matter required, but he was an Irish dude living in the 1890's, so it's more accurate to think of him getting all his information from, like... a couple of Eyewitness books he read at the school library one time, rather than an exhaustive well researched historical reference book. Also, y'know... racism. It was the 1890's, he was reading books written in English aboot Romanians... you have to take into account the racism part.

So basically what happened is that Stoker understood "Dracula" to be equal to "Draculesti," as in, a family name, which he believed meant "devil" and not "son of the devil/dragon," so he didn't really understand that it was a personal name adopted by a specific guy. The people who started publicizing the connection in the '70's were Romanians who were using the popularity of the novel to drum up interest in Romanian history. Which absolutely worked. As for the character in the novel, the historical background given in the text actually seems to suggest the character is intended to be Michael the Brave, although this is also pretty speculative.

Not that any of this matters anymore, as ever since the '70's there have been too many works based on Stoker's Dracula to count which explicitly connect the two. The fictional and historical Draculas are, at this point, inseparable, and given that Stoker did put in the effort to try and craft a very grounded story in a way where he could talk aboot these things with a level of understanding that was at least high enough to convince readers at the time that he knew what he was talking aboot, I'd say it's a continuation of his legacy to continue to draw more Romanian history and folklore into the story of the fictional Dracula.

TL;DR Stoker definitely had some knowledge of Dracula, but the popularity of his book and the criticism and commentaries that followed created a world where the general public today knows far, FAR more aboot the actual historical Dracula than Stoker ever did.

Author: @markusfreund6961
Content:
Heh it never ceases to amaze which words end up as loan words in God knows what parts of the world. "Hendl" is a word from southern German dialects (Palatian, Bavarian, not sure about Hessian, you get the idea), and since Austrian German is still a southern variety of German, that's probably how "Hendl" entered into the Balkan region via the Austrian-Hungarian Empire.
Interestingly (if you're a language nerd), a female chicken is called Huhn or Henne in German while a male one (aka a rooster) is called "Hahn". Bear with me. The diminutive of "Hahn" is "Hähnchen" ("little rooster") which, incidentally, is also the word for "broiled chicken"/"chicken roast". Whether "Hendl" derives from "Henne" or "Hähnchen" I do not know but it happens to be the southern German term for a prepared chicken, rather than a living one.
Imagine, as an American, finding "chuck roast" as a loan word in some obscure Aztec dialect, that's about how finding "Hendl" in a recipe from southeastern Europe is to me. 🤷‍♂🤓🍻

Content: A bottle labeled "Old Tokay" from the 1800s is a type of fortified dessert wine, most likely from the Tokaj region of Hungary. The most famous type is Tokaji Aszú, a sweet, rich dessert wine made from shriveled, nobly rotten grapes, affected by "noble rot", or, Botrytiscinerea, which adds to their complex flavor and sweetness, though other varieties like Szamorodni, a dry wine, were also produced. These wines were highly prized by royalty and are known for their rich, sweet, and complex flavors. Some bottles may be fortified with a distilled spirit, to make them more of a liqueur.  It was a favorite among European royalty and nobility for centuries, including Russian Tsars and Austrian Emperors, and was called "the wine of kings" by Louis XIV.

Author: @rzvn2007
Content:
Hello, I'm a huge fan from Romania! Love your work!
I am writing here though to provide a small correction.
At some point you mention the name "Dracula" was inspired from Vlad the Impaler, which is correct. You also say "Vlad Dracula, which at the time when Bram Stocker wrote the novel meant Devil", again, correct. 
The incorrect part is the name. The correct name was "Vlad Draculea" - In Romanian back then, adding "ea" to a name meant "of" - "Vlad son of Dracul".
His father was named "Vlad Dracul" - "Dracul" was a name he gained after joining "The order of the Dragon", and it comes from the latin for dragon - "Draco". Basically, it would translate to "Vlad the Dragon".
Therefore "Vlad the Impaler" by the form "Vlad Draculea" meant "Vlad son of the Dragon", not of the Devil.
Keep up the good work, I just love your videos!

Content: I grew up loving vampire lore and films; the most prominent was Bram Stoker's Dracula. However, I never paid much attention to what Jonathan ate on his trip. Later in life, I met a lovely Hungarian lady, who is now my wife, and I lived in Hungary for a while. Reading Dracula again much later, I was thrilled to discover that I have eaten most of the meals and drinks Harker had on his journey. Hungarian cuisine, along with dishes from surrounding countries, is fantastic! We still cook many Hungarian dishes at home today. Paprikash Csirke and Tarhonya Hus are some of my favorites. Palinka is like brandy—very strong, but pleasant after a few sips. The best Palinka I've had came from homemade stocks that I swear Hungarians serve out of habit when you visit. Takaj wine is excellent. Another underrated wine I really enjoy is the Riesling from around Lake Balaton. I often crave that taste. Thanks for this video! May you have a ghoulish All Hallows' Eve.

Content: I SPY RUDOLF JELÍNEK SLIVOVICE!!! You have no idea how happy it makes me to see plum brandy (slivovice in Czech) our most famous distillery makes in your video. They should properly be no less than 40% abv (80 proof) and can go as high as 60% (120 proof), sometimes 70% (140 proof) when in truly rural parts of the country. If you spy an older guy in a traditional ornamented outfit at a festival pouring you a colourless liquid from an unmarked glass bottle into a shot glass, steel yourself if youre gonna drink it. Its gonna be the best spirit youve ever had but your throat will be on fire. Its such a shame that our spirits rarely get talked about because aside from beer (Bohemia has best) and wine (Southern Moravia has best) fruit distilates are Northeastern Moravias best export.

Author: @slygirl0213
Content:
Chicken paprikash and Nokedli was the Sunday family staple meal at Nanas, her recipe was always made by heart and taste as ingredients were never identical in quality, freshness and storage. She was so heavy guarded on her recipe and sadly out of spite, no one got her personal one. After going through pages and pages of traditional Hungarian food bloggers it's taken a while to dial in the flavors I remember. 
Main take-away, don't guard family recipes that only end up dyeing along too. Passing down something so special like that is taken for granted, I would be so proud to continue passing on family recipes and knowledge that's been going for generations.

Content:
Also Max, the word Hen, in German means Hen, ie. Soup Hen, ie, boiler, not fryers, these were the chickens that were used for this dish. The reason being, they need longer times to cook. In America,  A "soup chicken" used to be called a "stewing chicken." This just means that it is an older, tougher bird that should be cooked using a slow-cooking or stewing method in order to soften up the meat.
Never use a Broiler Chicken to make Paprikahendl, it will turn to snot.

Content: The real Vlad would've been probably a vegetarian, he must've been because a number of reasons such as the colder climate than today, the droughts and the military campaigns. His story is full of violence and even hypocrisy thinking about it, but he was a fascinating character because of the legend and the scarcity of real information. "In Search Of Dracula" and "Dracula, Prince Of Many Faces" are great reads, they compile most of what people should know about the legends and the man. Since then, a lot more things were brought to light or corrected about Dracula but those books are awesome.

Content:
You felt the nokedli underwhelming because you plated the dish in the wrong way. Why you pour the gravy on the meat if you cooked it in it? It has enough already. Instead you should pour the gravy onto the nokedli. Et voila! The nokedli is really good in absorbing flavours. Be it a gravy or a soup, especially if the liquid contains paprika. This is why you mostly see nokedli inside gulyás, halászlé (fish soup) or beside stew or paprikas.
Sometimes called nokedli? In reality most people in Hungary call it nokedli. The galuska is its "official" name you may find in cookbooks, restaurant menues, etc.

Author: @AdamZovits
Content:
Some comments from a Hungarian:
 - Great job on the pronunciation, I think any of us would appreciate the effort you put into it :)
 - There is no such thing as too much paprika. You could easily add two or three times that amount.
 - Take care to avoid confusing paprikás csirke with the similarly named and made csirkepörkölt (that does not contain sour cream) or with csirkepaprikás (that does, but some people insist it is a different dish).
 - Tokaji is a... khm... interesting choice. A recommended wine pairing would be Pinot Noir, Kadarka or Kékfrankos. Maybe a rosé. But for all intents and purposes, do have a glass of Tokaji afterwards as dessert.
 - It is okay for the galuska to be bland, as it only serves to accompany the delicious sauce that adheres to it on the way to the mouth.
 - Despite your emphasis on not letting the meat fall apart, my wife and I agree that it is even desired to cook paprikás csirke until the bones fall cleanly out of the meat.
 - The dimensions of the galuska in the video place it on the category border to the Austrian / South German Spätzle - the Hungarian one is on the rounder, shorter side.

Author: @chopinfanclub6672
Content:
In late-Victorian England (when Dracula was written), “dinner” and “supper” were not always synonyms, and which one you used revealed class and context.

⸻

1. Class distinction
	•	For the upper and middle classes, “dinner” referred to the main formal meal of the day, typically in the evening.
	•	For working or country folk, “dinner” was the midday meal, while the lighter evening meal was called “supper.”

So when Jonathan Harker (the solicitor) writes in his journal, he’s probably realizing mid-sentence that in his current situation — traveling in rural Transylvania, eating late at night in an inn — it’s more accurate, and perhaps more modest or provincial, to call it “supper.”
He starts with his polite English habit (“dinner”) and then corrects himself to reflect the local or situational reality (“or rather, supper”).

Author: @powellmountainmike8853
Content: My grandmother was born in Slovakia in 1892, when it was still part of Austria-Hungary. The place where she lived was very near the Hungarian border, and some of the words in the family dialect are Hungarian, not standard Slovak. The family came to the U.S. just before World War One.  One of the recipes she brought with her is for chicken paprikash. It is VERY similar to that described in the old cookbook, except it uses sweet cream in the gravy, not sour cream, and butter for the fat. It is best made with real Hungarian paprika, half sweet, half hot, not the generic kind found in most American supermarkets which is Spanish paprika. As to the halushki, she always said they should be small, like the end of your little finger, not as big as your thumb. The recipe for them is similar but simpler, flour eggs and milk (and I add a tablespoon of baking powder) for the thick batter, almost a dough, which you cut off a cutting board into the boiling salted water with a wet knife.  make them in handy batches; and, once the batch has cooked long enough to all rise to the top of the water, scoop them out with a strainer ladle, and put them into the chicken and paprika dish. Once all the halushki are cooked and in the chicken paprikash let them cook with the other ingredients over very low heat, just keeping on a very slow simmer, for at least a half hour so all the flavors can meld. In my mind, I can see my grandmother making this dish on the old Mealmaster wood stove that formed the heart of her kitchen. I still make this recipe today. It is one of my favorites.

Author: @ErikZiak
Content: Now that looks almost like the Paprikáš that I make. I let the chicken almost fall apart, take it out and let cool down a little. Then I pull the meat from the bones and make sure to remove any gristle that might be stuck to the meat as well. While the meat is cooling down after being taken from the pot, I add cream, bring the pot to a boil, then lower the heat and thicken the sauce with a flour and butter "paste" and let that simmer for a minute. Then I remove the heat, add the "pulled chicken" and give it a final taste. Depending on taste you can add a little lemon juice or salt. The galushki, or halušky as we call them, are the "simple" flour based side-dish version (there is a more elaborate and labor intensive version made with potatoes and without eggs). A very good side dish especially in the case of a paprikáš. If the type of meat is not specified, a paprikáš is expected to be from chicken. But there are also version with rabbit meat, called rabbit paprikáš.

Ok, so I have to share this bit if history whenever the subject of Dracula is brought up. I just can’t help myself, it’s so interesting.

Bela Lugosi, who played Dracula in the classic 1931 film, was a special ops soldier.

He joined the Austro-Hungarian army when WW1 broke out and initially served as an infantry officer, seeing heavy combat against the Russians. Later, he joined a Ski-Patrol unit. A sort of proto-special forces unit like the Sturmtruppen or Arditi. They specialized in mountain warfare, long range reconnaissance, and occasionally raiding.

He was also the officer in charge of executions of criminal and deserter soldiers. Which caused him to suffer a mental breakdown in 1916 that saw him med boarded out of the army.

20 years after his performance as Dracula, another special operations veteran would take up the mantle of Dracula. Christopher Lee.

Content:
The noodles are made very much like Spätzle, as others have noted here and in the comments on Facebook.  In fact, the tool you used to make them is sold as a Spätzlehobel, a Spätzle grater.  There are presses, too, designed like a garlic press.  The traditional way is to put the dough on a board and scrape bits of it into a pot of boiling water with the back edge of a knife. I use a press, because I haven't mastered the scraping technique.  I like to add a teaspoon of farina to my dough, for some texture, and nutmeg.

And more literary trivia, regarding Tokay. In the "Adventures of Baron Munchausen", the Baron visits Constantinople.  He wagers with the Sultan-the Baron's head,against as much treasure as the strongest man can carry,  if he cannot produce, within an hour, a bottle of the finest Tokay from the Imperial cellars in Vienna. Of course, the Baron wins the bet.

Stoker accurately picked up that detail in his novel.

Author: @ilyencsaknincs
Content:
Hungarian from the Great Plain here. Thanks a lot for bringing already the second Hungarian dish on your show after gulyás. And a special hat-tip for taking the time and effort to properly pronounce Hungarian words! Just a little correction on the side dish: it's a common misconception that galuska,  nokedli and Spätzle are the same. The side dish in the video is vajasgaluska(=butter galuska) which is indeed similar to nokedli in shape but nokedli has neither butter nor milk in it. It's made only with 4 ingredients: plain flour, egg, water and salt and is more commonly eaten in Hungary with pörkölt and paprikás than vajasgaluska. Or it can be a standalone dish, e.g. tojásos nokedli (egg nokedli). 
As for Spätzle, it's made also with flour, water egg and salt but is more part of the German/Austrian cuisine than of the Hungarian. For example Käsespätzle is a star. 
One note on the wine:  Kadarka and other light red wines are great with chicken paprikás. 
Anyway, thanks again for the great recipes and histories, and please keep bringing Central European dishes and stories. 🤗

Content: Cat meat man..There is a special German dish for horse meat called sour roast. It is known since the Roman period at the river Rhine, especially in Cologne, a former Roman settlement. The meat has to be marinated one week in spices, vinegar or wine and water. The history goes that the romans used this method to give meat a longer shelf life. In fact the horse meat will become tender and tastes less like horse. If you read a recipe you will find that the spices, thickeners (some sort of ginger bread) and sweetener are truly medieval, even raisins will be added to the sauce. Nowadays horse is still at the menu in that area but most people would prefer the version with beef and wine. So yes, in former times people would have taken the horse while cats had to go after mice and get the unwanted cuts from the kitchen. My cat prefers rabbit in sauce out of a can.

Author: @UtiuNikita
Content:
As a romanian born in Bistritz/Bistrita, you cannot imagine how happy it makes me that you covered this dish. My mom would often cook this and this is pretty much synonymous with comfort food for me.

One of details I enjoyed when reading the book is how Bram Stoker  highlighted how much of a cultural melting pot Transylvania is - fact that is very much reflected in its cuisine being a mix of Central, Eastern and South-Eastern European dishes. Even nowadays, it's quite common to see, side-by-side, a mix of borsch-like sour soups ("ciorbe"), Turkish-style dishes like "sarmale", and schnitzels.

As a sidenote - "impletata" could also refer to "împletită" meaning "braided", which makes me think that the author was referring to one of the many "colac"/"kalach" style breads and pies eaten in Eastern and Central Europe (the jewish Callah is an example of this). I've had it many times before, either plain or with some savory stuffing like cheese.

Author: @zekesanonymity
Content: Slivovitz has the nickname of Jewish Whiskey.  Think of a couple old guys sipping it while BSing on a park bench in winter.  It's potent, but makes for a great booze to mix into cocktails and spritzers as its fruit flavor gets more notable when thinned by carbonated beverages and gets less potent.  Even something like Sprite and ice gets tasty when you add a bit of Slivovitz.  It's a fairly unknown booze by youth today, but deserves more appreciation if mixology is your thing.  In eastern Europe it was made because harvest season left farmers with a choice between using valuable grain for booze or this mass of plums that had already saturated store shelves and home jam makers.  So they fermented the leftovers of the plum harvest, rather than waste grain that stored longer.

Author: @williamgechtman9287
Content:
If it was *"old"* tokaji it would be somewhat less sweet. When young it is *very* sweet and *very* high in acidity. Over the decades the two merge and it becomes "rounder," for lack of a better term, but neither as sweet nor as acidic. Less spikey. The flavors merge.
No lesser a  personage than Louis XIV called tokaji "King of wines, Wine of kings."
Remember, this originated in the 15th century when there was not much sweetness in the world. Literally. No sugarcane plantations in the Caribbean or South America. Sweetness was a luxury, and tokaji had it in spades, if you made it properly for that purpose.

Content: Just some correction about the slivovice: That particular brand is from a family company, called Rudoph Jelinek and they come from Czech Republic. They started in 1894, and they were pretty of the other end of the Austro-Hungarian Empire then Transylvania. What the couch driver refer to, is more likely closer to Hungarian pálinka/Balkan rakija/Romanian cujka, which is a clear, non-aged fruit spirit made from a wide variety of fruit, not just plum (apple, apricot, peach, cherry, pear, etc). What he actually drink is an oak-barrel aged (10 years aging), plum fruit spirit (on sidenote, it is kosher, so Jewish people could enjoy it), so it is not quite period accurate. But, as a bartender, who works in a beer pub, which sells Czech beers and spirits,  I would say, this a pretty fine drink

Food history note: sweet paprika wasn't popularized in Hungary until after Dracula was written. The "thirsty dish" he ate used hot paprika that was probably considerably spicier than current Hungarian tastes. That's why he has to drink all his water and suspected it messed with his sleep.

You made modern paprikash which is great but if people want to try the dish from the time in Dracula they will need to alter it to add enough heat to make them drink all their water!

Changes in spice levels makes for a tough but fun history deep dive that requires a lot of detective work where recipes are often misleading, really sad you missed this one!

Author: @revgregory
Content:
A very good friend's father was originally from Hungary so this brought back some good memories.  They ran a winery for several decades and once a year we would set up at a large wine festival in the Poconos for the weekend but Opa would stay behind to run the wine shop while we were at the fest.  Sunday after the fest ended we would bring everything back to the winery and put it away and Opa would have a meal ready for us which was almost always paprikash csirki and Spätzle.  Oma made the noodles and she was German so we didn't call them nokedli, you didn't dare mix the names up if you knew who had made them even though they were basically them same thing!  Of course there were always rounds of Šljivovica shots to celebrate a long weekend of work, although the house beer was the very American Yuengling which Opa was quite fond of which was fine with me. 

As an aside, Opa often used the somewhat generic term "palinka" to encompass Šljivovica and the many other fruit brandies from Eastern Europe.  According to him the difference between the Hungarian varieties and others was that it was only true Hungarian palinka if the fruit it was made from was stolen...LOL!

Author: @McJays
Content: Hi Max, I'm Jay from Transylvania. The german town/city name is Klausenburg (burg=old walled city; berg=mountain), or Cluj in romanian, the old unofficial capital of Transylvania (and the biggest city. It's where I and thousands of others went to University). And by the way, I live maybe 20 km (12.5 miles) from the town of Mediaș (Mediash). The transylvanian saxsons (my mother is one and I consider myself one as well) used to divide the land of Transylvania into agricultural areas, based on what produce would grow best there. They calld this area where we live Weinland (the land of wine), basically the plateau between the 2 Târnava rivers (the great/big Târnava and the lesser/small Târnava), because the best produce they cultivated here in large quantity (hundreds of hectares) were grapes, both for the table and for winemaking . Even today, everybody that owns a house, have a grapevine in their yards, and in a village called Jidvei, not far from Mediaș, they still produce wine on an industrial scale. In 2014, (if I remember right) they got a worldwide prize/diploma for the best cabernet sauvignon red wine. It is a very good wine; I can reccomend both it and any other (cheaper) wines made at Jidvei. I think they export them in the U.S. as well.

Author: @MrVokiman
Content:
Because you mentioned adding other things like spices to the galushka, over here in Austria we usually don't have mac and cheese, instead we have Käsespätzle.
All you need is galushka/Spätzle, diced onions, optional salt and pepper and of course grated cheese (Käse). Usually people use a hard cheese with a strong flavour.
Just chuck everything into a pan with a bit of oil so it doesn't burn and fry it until the cheese gets crispy, so if you take it out you have both crispy and melted cheese in one dish.
It's a very hearty, simple meal and probably one of Austria's most iconic traditional dishes.
Though be warned that the whole house is going to smell what you are cooking.

Author: @AtomicPrimate-h4d
Content: Interesting fact is that in the book Dracula himself cooked and prepared every meal served at his castle. I had always assumed that he made the paprikash "thirsty" on purpose, with the intention of imparting a taste of what Dracula's own never ending thirst, his anguish, was like upon his guest. He was just that kind of a guy. But anyway, Chicken Paprikash is one of the best dishes the human species has ever devised. And certainly one of my all time favorites. I'm not Hungarian, but my mom's first husband was, and HIS mom had immigrated to the usa back in the 50s bringing with her all of her wonderful classic recipes. So she taught my mom, and then after they divorced and she remarried, my mom taught me. The only 2 things that seem to be different between the 50s version that I learned and still make, and this older version is that in the 50s version you would lightly flour the chicken and fry it brown in the added chicken fat. Remove it, deglaze the pan, then you build your sauce with a little bit of cream as well as sour cream, add the chicken back and let it simmer. Also, we always used two kinds of paprika. Lots and lots and I do mean LOTS of sweet paprika, (the dish should be deep red not pink) and just a small dash of hot paprika (just like Dracula probably did). And today, I like to also add just a bit of smoked paprika as well. The dumplings are spot on identical to the modern versions. And by the way are quite a nice paring with a wide range of saucy dishes. Now as for wine, even though it's chicken it's normally pared with a red wine. Something not candy sweet, but not bone dry either and with good strong fruit notes.

Content: During my university time, I unearthed a manuscript from 1732, which recounts the official investigation of an alleged vampire outbreak in Serbia in January of the same year. If you want to read it, it's part of the manuscript collection of the Friedrich Alexander University in Erlangen. To dampen your expectations just a bit: While it's quite gouhlish with exhumations and everything, it's very much laced with the usual superstition - and after reading it, a few physician friends of mine, when presented with the findings of the investigator, didn't take a minute to recognize the symptoms as arsenic poisoning. The symptoms were remarkably similar to those you describe, undecomposed body, fresh bright red "blood", and possibly seemingly growing nails and teeth too? Yes, those are the symptoms of arsenic poisoning. You see, the seemingly growing nails and teeth are a thing it all corpses: The dessication pulls back the flesh, making the nails and teeth seem longer.

I've tried a version of csirkepaprikás with a mix of sweet and hot paprika and a tablespoon of paprikakrém (from a tube like tomato paste, but paprika) that is added once the chopped onions have cooked in oil for a while. To keep the dry paprika from burning, some wine and then stock is added. Added also one chopped red bell pepper and one chopped tomato. And the chicken, obviously. 
After it had cooked almost the full time, sour cream was added, but no flour. 
Instead of thickening the soup with flour, the liquid "soup" and cooked vegetables got blended in the pan. This led to an amazing consistency of a thick but not too thick sauce. 
Serve the dish with cold sour cream so everyone can add to taste also adjust acidity more or less. 

And yes, the smell and taste was unbelievably good.

Author: @madalinadelia
Content:
Actually.... Vlad the Impaler (Vlad Tepes) did not drink the blood of his victims. Bram Stoker's novel, Dracula, only used Vlad's nickname in his novel and nothing else.
Countess Elizabeth Báthory of Ecsed was a Hungarian noblewoman and alleged serial killer from the powerful House of Báthory, who owned land in the Kingdom of Hungary (now Slovakia). Legends describing her vampiric tendencies, such as the tale that she bathed in the blood of virgins to retain her youth, were based on rumours and only recorded as supposedly factual over a century after her death. These stories were repeated by at least three historians in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.  Some insist that Elizabeth's story inspired Bram Stoker's novel Dracula (1897).
And this is where the blood drinking came to be in the novel Dracula. It is a mish-mash of information from a variety of countries.

Content:
I have googled a bit and apparently people nowadays may call nokedli galuska.  Wow. I never will do it, I have learned the apparently original distinction, galuska is bigger and we use a spoon to make the pieces. But people often make the dough differently anyway. I mostly make galuska, never use water or milk, just egg as water source. But for this dish, nokedli is the norm and that's fine too. (My Golash has galuska while others use different pasta or nothing at all, one can always eat some bread with that soup though some pasta never kept the bread lovers to have both.)
But the csirkepaprikás is made like always - with personal differences as some people canát make a stew without tomato and pepper and garlic (that isn't my style). And the flour was a surprise to me but it's a tiny difference as it's such a tiny amount.

We wanted to make some stew next time (same as this dish but with pork and sour cream would be an option, probably not used) but I haven't had this dish since... Maybe more than a decade or two so maybe we will make this one. Author: @Vilyan
Content: To be honest, I like this video buuut, I had the honor of talking with Dacre Stoker and he told me about the creation of Dracula. Most of the characters are actually inspired by his life directly. By his father and his employer. He did very few researches on Romania / Transilvania. He went to a library where he found a book about myths and traditions from Transylvania. So he'd mostly based his work around that. Dracula is a very debated word - it did and does not mean "devil"  directly. "drac, or drac(ul)" means the devil but Dracula comes either from his father's sir name Draculea from the House of Draculesti orrrrr, as drak in slavic meant "dragon", and because he and his dad were members of the Order of the Dragon, could be that Dracula derived from that. Either way, Bram associated the words and gave it a new meaning.  Regarding the dishes, indeed, the entire land was part of Hungary and the food certainly had Hungarian origins. Even though Romania was monarchy back when Bram was writing the book, parts of it were still under the Austro-Hungarian scepter. Hope this clarifies the information a bit! <3 Love from Timisoara!

Author: @mags9024
Content:
Well this is the first episode of Tasting History that has ever made me cry. My father passed away when I was a young child and his mother was from Transylvania. His parents were immigrants who fled the Austro-Hungarian Empire at the start of WW1. I have only one memory of visiting my grandmother as a toddler and she spoke to me in her Transylvanian accent laced with affectionate bits of  Romanian. I have made this dish regularly throughout my life to maintain a feeling of connection with that side of my history (originally from a cookbook she gave my mother). 
On a lighter note, my father used to chase my mom around and pretend he was a vampire to make her laugh. I actually had to stifle a fit of giggles as a kid kneeling by his coffin because he looked exactly like the classic Hollywood depiction of Dracula. TLDR: Fave episode. I have a morbid sense of humor but I make great chicken.

"Schmalz" is not only chicken fat in German but every kind of semi-hardened animal fat.
There's "Schweineschmalz" (pork lard) "Rinderschmalz" (beef lard) and the best of all "Gänseschmalz" (goose lard).
It's common to eat the latter on our dark German "Schwarzbrot/Pumpernickel" with salt, pepper and pickeled cucumber.
Classic German pub food.

Author: @davidh9844
Content: Again, fun episode! RE: Tokaj wine. We lived in Northern Italy for a number of years, in the Po Valley. Historically this part of the Veneto was not part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, but we were close enough. At the time, there were only two grapes grown in the Veneto for everyday, bottle capped table wine. For the common folks and us impoverished students: Merlot for red (ghastly) and Tokaj (white). Over the years, much more became available, but then Tokaj was our go to. Next Slivovitz, plum brandy. As you know from your Latke episode, the lives of the Jews and the Locals were very closely intertwined in Central and Eastern Europe. During Passover, most distilled spirits were forbidden because they were made from fermented grains. Fruit, however, was allowed (we love to split hairs...) Slivovitz became a traditional drink during Passover because it is distilled plums. My family never partook, but I learned about slivovitz being fire water from my friend Jerry way back when while I was in elementary school.

Content: I burst out laughing when you tasted the slivovice. I read somewhere that it's 100 proof - AFTER diluting it after distilling. My family came from what is now   Czechia and Slovakia (they all came over around 1900 give or take a few years either way), and the way my Czech grandparents used to drink it, it wasn't sippin' brandy. It was a shot down the hatch, slam the shot glass on the table, and follow it with a beer! (And yes, this was Grandma as well as Grandpa.)  My Mom and her sisters often made paprikas, but my Mom preferred to make veal paprikas rather than chicken. The little dumplings in your dish look like German spaetzle and Slovak halušky. You owe it to yourself to make bryndzové halušky, Slovakia's national dish/comfort food: small, soft, chewy potato dumplings coated in bryndza, a fermented fresh sheep cheese, and topped with fried bacon pieces and bacon drippings.

In that Time it wouldn't have been unusual at all to hear german spoken in Translyvania, it was after all ruled by austria for many centuries. About 800 Years ago they brought in a whole lot of settlers from germany to defend against Invasions from central asia, the Transylvanian-Germans or as we call ourselves Siebenbürger Sachsen.

Most cities in transylvania have german and romanian names, the city that Max mentions, Klausenburg (called Cluj in Romanian), has a very tasty dish named after them the "Klausenburger Kraut", a Sauerkraut Lasagna in a way, mince meat, rice sauerkraut and schmand are layered and baked in the oven. 

My family "had" a vineyard near Medias and my Dad actually took some of the plants and planted them when we moved to germany. He still makes wine as a hobby.

I would love an Episode about Transylvanian Saxons. Our traditions and History will die out in a few decades, since we are too split up geographically to keep up and we young people don't really care to be involved in Tradition Clubs (Landsmannschaften idk how to translate that).

Well at least I can pass on some of it to my nieces and nephews, in food and recipes.

Content: I have to disagree about the sweet paprika comment for this time period. While it is used today, sweet paprika wasn't developed  until about 30 years before Dracula was published. From a consumer market perspective, it didn't become widely available until 1897. This means the more traditional hot paprika would have been used when the author writing this passage in the book. His comments of "thirsty," fistful dreams, and need for drink alluded to the heat of the paprika and how his bland British palate couldn't handle the heat. It also set the stage for the hellish destiny he was traveling towards. So, the author was using food as allusion for what was to transpire.

Author: @FTWIHA
Content:
"Galuschka" and "Nokedli" are actually two different things.
"Nokedli" in the Hungarian way of writing "Nockerln", which is the Austrian name for "Knöpfle" which in turn are Swabian/Allemanic (Southern German) "Spätzle", a type of small egg dumpling, that are strained instead of stripped off a board.
Galuschka on the other hand is the Hungarian way of writing, well, "Galushka", which is a similar but distinctly different type of dumpling common throughout all the Slavic cultures that is made without egg, using cottage cheese instead.

What you made was a distinctly Austro-Hungarian variant of Nokedli / Nockerln (no other variety contains milk) that is usually eaten as desert in a thick cream-based sauce sweetened with sugar (or honey) and fruits.
This is the first time i've ever seen them prepared as a side dish like this.
Due to the very distinct history of Transylvannia (having been influenced heavily by culturally and ethnically by Slavic, Hungarian and German aspects while being Romance/Romanic) these two (or i guess three) dishes seem to have melted into one distinctly Transylvanian variety.

Definitively have to try that and see how the milk influences the flavour!

Author: @erzsebetkovacs2527
Content: Yay, Hungarian food and wine on the channel! So happy to see you make it from a classic Hungarian recipe, the way it is still made in Hungarian households. You don't need to take the onions that far, though, they only need to cook until translucent, and then you can add the rest of the "pörkölt" ingredients, even some chopped tomato and/or chopped raw peppers, if you want to have a more substantial sauce with your meat. Like I said, this is basically "pörkölt", another dish from Hungarian cuisine. Somewhat confusingly, it's the addition of thickener (flour mixed in with sour cream), that makes this a paprikash, though. Calling it Hendl would have been appropriate at the time and place, indeed, because even though Hungarian was an official language of Austria-Hungary, German was much more widely spoken, including in Transylvania with its historical German settlers. Hendl refers to a very young chicken, but in fact, you could make the same dish with a larger and more mature hen, too, you just need to have it simmer longer. As for the egg noodles, galushka is the original Hungarian term, while "nokedli" is a Hungarianised form of Nockerl, which is the Austrian term for Spaetzle. They are kind of similar, too, but galushka is much smaller than the elongated Spaetzle and they are dressed and served in a different way. Galushka needs to be bland, so don't add any other spice or flavouring than salt, and using a neutral vegetable oil is also much more customary, because it only needs to carry the flavours of paprikash or beef "pörkölt" that it's served with. A regional variety of it comes from the regional cuisines of Northern Hungary (at the time) and Slovakia (now), which is made with grated raw potatoes and some flour, egg and neutral vegetable oil into a batter of similar consistency and cooked in boiling water in the same way. Those potato noodles are dressed either with cooked cabbages or cooked lardons and a regional variety of ewe's cheese. All of these combined pasta dishes are homely comfort foods, but I'm especially partial towards the very last one, served with chopped raw dill greens (when in season).

Content: I like to add in duck gizzard and some times chicken liver to my chicken paprikás. Duck gizzard needs a long time to soften so the cooking steps need adjustment. I start with heating lard then add the chicken to brown the skin a bit, then remove it and put it aside. Next add in the onions cook them then add paprika same as in the video. Next you add the gizzards and water, bring it to a boil then simmer at low heat for an hour or untill the gizzards soften, last time i had really tough gizzards that needed almost 2 hours. Add the chicken back in and simmer for 30 minutes. If you use chicken liver then add it last as it becomes tough if you overcook it.

Author: @THEPUFFY1231
Content: Man, I don't see any comments about it, so I guess I have to bring it up, huh? You mentioned that the Dracula story is told via travelogues: there's actual dates to almost every single entry, and that lead to someone going 'what if we presented the Dracula story with each entry on it's corresponding day?', leading to a fun email newsletter called Dracula Daily. Getting presented with roughly 1 entry per day ended up being a fun way to introduce folks to the Dracula story over the course of a year, and folks on Tumblr especially took a shine to the format. The travelogue opening was especially popular, reacting to it like they would a travel log. 'Opening my email to check out the latest letter from my Good Friend Johnathan as he goes through Transylvania to meet with some guy named Dracula :)'  I recall lot of folks made fun of Johnathan Harker for finding Paprika too spicy. There was a lot of debate on if it was just his Delicate English Diet or if Paprika in the 1800s genuinely was a lot more spicier then what folks associate with Paprika today, but personally I love that he goes right back to that Paprika for breakfast. The book and the Dracula Daily fandom definitely inspired me to try making Paprika Hendl and mamaliga myself to the best of my ability 😄I remember the mamaliga stood out to me with how it definitely felt like a 'poor man's dish' with how simple it was to cook; it was tasty though!

Author: @Elmonsoon
Content: The name Dracula is super interesting. There was an Order of the Dragon - a hyper Christian knightly order that Vlad's dad belonged to and he took a dragon as like his symbol.. so he got called Dracul. His son, Vlad, got called Son of the Dragon, which is Dracula. However, by the time  of Bram Stoker the symbol of the dragon no longer was associated with a Christian knightly order but with the devil - not helped by the reputation of Vlad. So the average uninformed person would have though the name Dracula was an association with the devil not associating him with a staunch defender of Christianity.
